interactions.summary: A student suggests that Piccarda confines herself to the lower sphere because she never fully forgives herself, and Jiang pivots from that answer into the proverb 'where there is a will there is a way' to ask what stronger willing would have required.
Students unpack the proverb by saying a person who truly wills escape imagines a path out and, in some sense, draws reality into alignment with that imagined route.

Jiang formalizes the class's answer into a metaphysics of will: intense desire produces an idea, the universe responds to that imaginative act, and Piccarda's failure shows insufficient faithfulness rather than external impossibility alone.

claims.claim: Jiang reframes Piccarda's placement by saying the issue is not simply that her vow was broken but that she did not will escape strongly enough to generate a path beyond coercion.
The class defines 'where there is a will there is a way' as a process in which genuine will first imagines a route and then reality or the universe bends enough to let that route be enacted.
topic_tags: where there is a will there is a way

claims.claim: Jiang says Piccarda's limitation is a failure of fidelity: if she had really wanted escape, an idea would have arrived and the universe would have opened the way.
The student's suggestion that Piccarda 'confined herself' implies that heavenly placement is partly self-imposed through inner consent rather than only assigned from outside.

signature_moments.moment: The class turns will into a world-shaping force: imagine the path strongly enough and the universe starts furnishing the way.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest move from moral judgment into a metaphysics of manifestation and cosmic response.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says Piccarda's real failure is not broken vows but not being 'faithful enough' to want escape all the way through.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This compresses his reinterpretation of the entire lower-sphere problem into one severe standard of desire.

glossary_terms.term: where there is a will there is a way
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The proverb Jiang uses as a bridge from Piccarda's case into a theory that strong enough willing generates both imagination and a route of escape.
Jiang's criterion for whether a person truly wills salvation or freedom rather than merely wishing for it weakly.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet marks the turn from the Piccarda paradox into a positive model of will, where imagination and cosmic response become the mechanism explaining heavenly stagnation.

uncertainty_notes.note: The opening student line is clipped and may carry more context about self-forgiveness than the ASR preserves, so extraction keeps only the stable idea of self-confinement.
